anomalous

/uh-NOM-uh-lus/ — stress on second syllable, similar to marvelous · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is anomalous is different from what is normal or expected.

The scientists rechecked the anomalous reading; no other sensor showed it.

Example

The biologist discovered an anomalous species of frog with six legs instead of four, forcing her to completely reconsider her data and field observations.

Anomalous is more precise than 'unusual' because it means something breaks a system's rules or expected pattern—not just different, but wrong according to the established system. 'Unusual' just means surprising.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

abnormal: Abnormal compares one thing with what is normal or healthy for its kind, and it is the usual word in medical settings — abnormal cells, an abnormal heartbeat. Anomalous compares one result with the pattern everything else follows: the lone exception that breaks the expected rule.

atypical: Atypical says something does not fit the usual profile of its kind — an atypical career path, an atypical answer — and it stays mild and general. Anomalous is sharper and more technical: it marks the one exception that breaks a system's expected pattern and demands an explanation.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

normal: matching the usual, expected pattern

typical: showing the usual traits of its kind

Where it sits · how far it breaks the expected pattern

normal → strange → irregular → anomalous

normal vs. anomalous: Normal is the opposite end of the scale from anomalous: a normal result fits the expected pattern exactly, while an anomalous one breaks it.

strange vs. anomalous: Strange is weaker and vaguer than anomalous; strange just means odd, while anomalous specifically marks the odd one out against an expected pattern or rule.

irregular vs. anomalous: Irregular is close but milder than anomalous: an irregular result varies a little from the pattern, while an anomalous one stands out as a clear exception that demands explanation.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — an-: not, without (Greek)

Root — omal: even, uniform (from Greek homalos, built on homos, 'same'; its h drops after the prefix)

Suffix — -ous: full of, possessing the quality of (Latin, via French)

Put it together: An- ('not') + omal ('even, uniform,' from Greek homalos — the h drops after the prefix) + -ous ('possessing the quality of') literally means 'not even, not uniform' — anomalous describes something that fails to match the normal, expected pattern.

Use the root in a new word: homophone: Jenna keeps a list of homophones taped inside her notebook so she stops mixing them up in essays.

Word Choice

formal / technical

Anomalous is the right choice when something breaks a system's rules or pattern in a technically significant way. For everyday strangeness, 'unusual' or 'strange' is simpler and better.
